The Speech
It's April 2034. On Saturday the “Ingrid-Brandt-Platz” sign will be unveiled. Ludwig has to give a short speech. Susanne helps him write it, with “beautiful” connectors.
So, Ludwig. Start. What did Ingrid do for the children?
She helped them. She read with them. Every day.
Good. Now in one sentence: “She helped the children by reading with them every day.” With “indem” you say how she did it.
“Indem sie las.” That sounds nice. Like a book title.
And then you have to say that the ceremony is outside. But only if the weather is good.
“We'll celebrate outside, provided it doesn't rain. Unless Elif decides otherwise.” She's the one organising everything, after all.
Perfect. And the man from Marzahn who wants to recite the poem? He told me he's scared. He still stutters sometimes when he's nervous.
As a child he could barely say his own name, let alone recite a poem. And now he's coming from Marzahn to read Brecht in front of two hundred people. That has to go in the speech.
And how long should the speech be?
Depending on how long I can go without crying. Three minutes, if I'm lucky. One, if not.
Then we'll write three minutes, although you can stop at any time. Nobody will complain, especially since most of them will be crying too.
Ingrid hated long speeches, whereas I always admired them. I'll keep it short. That's how she would have wanted it.

1. indem / dadurch, dass: the means
“indem” answers the question “how? by what means?”. The subject is usually the same in both clauses:
She helped the children by reading with them.
“dadurch, dass” has the same meaning and is useful when you want to put “dadurch” in the main clause: “Dadurch, dass sie las, lernten die Kinder.”
English often uses “by” + -ing: “by speaking it”, “by reading”. German has no such -ing form, so you use “indem”.
2. wobei, zumal, wohingegen
wobei
adds a restriction / a comment
Die Feier war schön, wobei es etwas kalt war.
zumal
reinforces a reason (especially since)
Er war gerührt, zumal so viele gekommen waren.
wohingegen
strong contrast (whereas)
Sie hasste lange Reden, wohingegen er sie liebte.
All three introduce a subordinate clause: verb at the end.
3. sofern, es sei denn, je nachdem
sofern
provided that (formal for “wenn”)
Wir feiern draußen, sofern es nicht regnet.
es sei denn, (dass)
unless (exception)
Wir feiern draußen, es sei denn, es regnet.
je nachdem, ob / wie / wann
Je nachdem, wie das Wetter ist, feiern wir draußen oder drinnen.
insofern, als
Das stimmt insofern, als sie nie aufgegeben hat.
After “es sei denn” there is usually a main clause (verb in 2nd position): “…, es sei denn, es regnet.” With “dass”, the verb goes to the end: “…, es sei denn, dass es regnet.”
4. geschweige denn
“geschweige denn” comes after a NEGATIVE clause and adds something even harder to imagine (= let alone):
I don't have time to cook, let alone bake.
The colloquial English equivalent: “let alone”.

Lehrerin und Leserin

The unveiling took place on Saturday, the twenty-second of April, at eleven o'clock, and the weather kept to Elif's plan, even though until ten it looked as if it would rain. From six in the morning Elif had checked the forecast three times, argued twice with her mother about whether she had to take her rain jacket, and called Mr Hartwig, the local councillor, once — he had meanwhile become her most ardent ally — to tell him to be on time, especially since he was bringing the scissors. At half past ten the sun came out from behind the clouds. Elif later claimed she had ordered it.

From seven o'clock Lena and Andrei were in the little square, with coffee from the café, with chairs, with a small table for the speakers. Mara and Jakob had hung garlands between the stop and the young chestnut tree, and Kuba and Ola, fourteen by now and far too cool to admit they were happy, handed out programmes that Elif had printed on the photocopier at school. At the very top of the programme, in Elif's round handwriting, it said: “Please do not cry before the sign has been unveiled.” Nobody kept to that.

The little square next to the stop was full of people, more than two hundred, as Katrin Krüger later wrote in the paper, although she admitted that at some point she had stopped counting. Former pupils of Ingrid Brandt had come from all over Germany: the linguistics professor from Toronto, who had booked a flight especially; a woman from Rostock with her three grandchildren; a group of five grey-haired men who had been in Ingrid's class together in 1981 and hadn't seen each other since. They only recognised each other when one of them said: “Mrs Brandt was always telling me to stop looking out of the window.” And the other four answered in chorus: “She told all of us that.”

Even Michael had come from Munich, with his mother, Renate, who crossed the square on Ludwig's arm as if they were old friends, which by now they were. And Thomas stood with Anja at the edge, by the chestnut tree, looking over at his father, and when Ludwig looked back, Thomas raised his hand, as Ludwig hadn't done at the window in 1997.

Susanne had already come from Hanover on Friday, with Peter and a bag full of copies: all two hundred and twelve letters, bound into a thick book she had had made at a print shop in Hanover, for Ludwig. On the cover it said: “Indem sie las. Letters to Ingrid Brandt.” She had stolen the title from Ludwig, as she admitted, from the conversation about his speech. Ludwig held the book on his knees throughout the ceremony, with both hands on it, as if he were afraid someone might take it away from him.

Ludwig sat in the front row, on a chair Lena had brought from the café, in his dark grey Sunday suit, with the sheet with his speech in his jacket pocket and the old brass bell in the other. Next to him sat Grete, ninety-seven years old, in black, with her pearl necklace, out among people again for the first time since Friedrich's death. She had said she would come only on condition that nobody expected her to give a speech or to smile. Then she had seen Elif, running between the chairs with her clipboard and giving instructions like a little general, and had smiled after all.

The district mayor spoke first, briefly and warmly. Then Mr Hartwig spoke, the councillor who in November had still been against it. He talked, without notes, about the box with the two hundred and twelve letters and how, on the weekend after the first meeting, he had read them all, one after the other, until three in the morning. “I was wrong,” he said, in front of two hundred people, in front of the camera that was filming. “And I'm glad of it. Because by being wrong, I found my own teacher again.” He pointed to a very old woman in a wheelchair at the edge of the square, with a woollen blanket on her knees. She was ninety-three. Her name was Mrs Lindner. He had visited her at the care home in December, for the first time in fifty years, and every Sunday since.

Then it was Ludwig's turn. He stood up, slowly, leaning on his stick, and Andrei helped him take the two steps to the microphone. He took the sheet out of his pocket, put on his glasses, looked at the paper. And then he folded it up again and put it back. “Susanne helped me write a very beautiful speech,” he said. “With lots of beautiful words. Indem, wobei, zumal. But Ingrid hated long speeches. So I'll say just three sentences.”
A blackbird landed on the covered sign, as if it wanted to be the first to find out what was written underneath, and only flew away when Ludwig stood up.

My wife was a primary school teacher. For forty years she taught children to read, by reading with each one of them, until they no longer needed her. And she once told me: whoever reads is never completely alone. Today I see that she was right. She isn't alone. You are all here.

It was more than three sentences. Nobody counted. Ludwig sat down again, and Grete put her hand on his arm without a word. Then a man of about sixty-five stepped forward, tall, with a grey beard and a crumpled book in his hand. His name was Rainer Brückner and he came from Marzahn. As a child he had stuttered so badly that at school he couldn't get a single word out, let alone a poem. Mrs Brandt had read with him for a whole year, every day after lessons. Now he stood in front of two hundred people, his hands trembling, and opened the book.

The first words wouldn't come. He opened his mouth and nothing came out. One second. Two. Three. The square went very quiet. Rainer Brückner closed his eyes. And then someone in the crowd said, very quietly, the first line of the poem. It was a woman from Rostock. Then a man from the group of five said the second line together with her. Then the professor from Toronto. And suddenly twenty, thirty, fifty of Ingrid Brandt's former pupils were reciting the poem together, quietly, in chorus, Brecht's “In Praise of Learning”, which they had all learned by heart with her forty or fifty years ago. And at the third verse Rainer Brückner opened his eyes and recited along with them. Without stuttering.

“Learn the simplest things! For those whose time has come, it is never too late!” He said the last line alone, loud and clear, and when he had finished he closed the book and looked at the ground, and two hundred people applauded for so long that the next tram stopped at the stop and the driver didn't move on, but looked out of the cab to see what was happening. It was Leo. He was in the first year of his apprenticeship and was already allowed, under supervision, to drive the occasional run. He saw his grandfather in the front row, saw the covered sign, saw the people, and rang the bell twice. As he had promised.

Then Elif pulled the cord. The green cloth fell. And on the new blue street sign, right next to the stop, by the young chestnut tree that was just putting out its first light-green leaves, it said in white letters: “Ingrid-Brandt-Platz”. And underneath, smaller, on a second sign, as Ludwig had wished: “Ingrid Brandt (1950–2021), teacher and reader. Whoever reads is never completely alone.” Ludwig looked at the sign for a long time without saying anything. Then he took the old brass bell out of his pocket and rang it, once, loud and clear, across the whole square. And Leo, in his tram, answered, twice.

Later, when most of the guests had left and only the family and the closest neighbours were still in the square, Mrs Lindner came over to Ludwig in her wheelchair, pushed by Mr Hartwig. She was very small and very old, and her voice could barely be heard. She took Ludwig's hand and said: “I knew your wife. Not well. We were on the same training course, in 1972, in Potsdam. She said there that if a child doesn't want to read, it just hasn't found the right book yet. I wrote it down. I told my pupils that for forty years.” Mr Hartwig looked at her in surprise. “You told me that too,” he said quietly. “In 1976.” Mrs Lindner smiled. “There, you see,” she said. “That's how it goes on. By passing it on.”

In the evening Ludwig sat alone in his flat, in Ingrid's armchair, with the thick book on his knees, reading. Not all the letters, just a few he didn't know yet. That evening, for the first time, he had moved the armchair to the front window, which looked out onto the street. Outside, in the little square in front of the stop, someone was sitting on one of the two benches under the new blue sign, reading a book. Ludwig couldn't see who it was. A stranger, perhaps, waiting for the tram. But he looked at him for a long time, at this person in Ingrid-Brandt-Platz who was reading, and thought: you see. He isn't alone.
